rows.label: Concept
rows.text: In-situ conservation guards species inside living ecosystems, through parks, reserves, buffer zones and sacred groves. Ex-situ conservation, in zoos, gardens and seed or gene banks, is the rescue layer when wild numbers collapse. Nepal's system, beginning with Chitwan in 1973, works only when reserves stay connected and local use around them is managed.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
In-situ sites: national parks, wildlife reserves, conservation areas, buffer zones, sacred groves.
Ex-situ sites: zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, gene banks, cryopreservation.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Ex-situ does not mean 'better protection'. It means protection away from the natural habitat. A zoo is ex-situ. A national park is in-situ.  ·  A seed bank saves plant genetic diversity. It does not save the insects, fungi and animals that lived with that plant.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Sacred groves count as in-situ. Students often leave them off the list.  ·  Gene banks store genetic material. They are ex-situ even when the species still has a wild population.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Chitwan National Park protects the greater one-horned rhinoceros in its floodplain habitat. That is in-situ.  ·  A seed bank holding local rice landraces is ex-situ conservation of crop diversity.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Buffer zones are not the core protected area. They are the surrounding land where limited use is allowed so that pressure on the core is reduced.  ·  Releasing zoo-bred animals succeeds only if the habitat they are returned to is still safe. Captive breeding without habitat protection does not restore the species.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Make a two-column table of in-situ and ex-situ with two Nepal examples.  ·  Explain one case where captive breeding must be paired with habitat protection.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: In-situ = in the site. Ex-situ = exit the site.  ·  Parks protect the play. Zoos and seed banks protect the actors off-stage.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: How does a buffer zone support the core of a national park?  ·  Why can captive breeding fail as a conservation plan if it is used alone?

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: A two-column answer, in-situ versus ex-situ, with two examples each, is the standard written question.  ·  Use a Nepal example (Chitwan, Sagarmatha, Annapurna, or a sacred grove) rather than only a foreign park.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: In-situ versus ex-situ  ·  National parks and buffer zones  ·  Seed banks and cryopreservation  ·  Sacred groves

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: In-situ: protect the species in its own habitat (parks, reserves, sacred groves).  ·  Ex-situ: protect it off-site (zoos, botanical gardens, seed and gene banks, cryopreservation).  ·  In-situ keeps ecological interactions and ongoing evolution.  ·  Ex-situ is the rescue option for critically endangered species and for crop varieties.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Nepal's protected-area system, including conservation areas and buffer zones, covers more than a fifth of the country's land.  ·  Cryopreservation stores semen, eggs, embryos or tissues at very low temperature, commonly in liquid nitrogen, so the cells remain viable for years.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Compare a botanical garden with a national park for protecting a rare orchid.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: The Central Zoo holding a breeding pair of a rare mammal is ex-situ. Returning their offspring to a guarded habitat joins the two strategies.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Which is an ex-situ method? → C  ·  In-situ conservation is preferred mainly because it → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: In-situ conservation protects a species inside the ecosystem where it already lives. The population keeps its predators, food, climate and the chance to keep evolving. National parks, wildlife reserves, conservation areas, buffer zones and sacred groves are in-situ tools.  ·  Ex-situ conservation removes individuals, seeds or genes from that habitat and keeps them under human care. Zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, gene banks, pollen banks and cryopreservation are ex-situ tools. It is the backup when the wild population is already too small.  ·  In-situ is preferred whenever the habitat can still be saved, because a captive population loses ecological relationships and can lose genetic variety. Ex-situ cannot replace a forest, but it can stop an immediate extinction and supply stock for a later release.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Isolation and edge effects  ·  Chitwan (1973) and Sagarmatha (1976) are landmark Nepali in-situ sites.  ·  Always state the limitation: ex-situ does not preserve the ecosystem.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Mention corridors or buffer zones when the question asks how to make a park actually work.  ·  In-situ conservation is the primary strategy because it protects the whole community, not one species in isolation.  ·  Ex-situ conservation is complementary: it preserves genes and individuals when the wild habitat is failing.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A reserve that is too small or too isolated loses species even if hunting is banned.  ·  Sort these into in-situ or ex-situ: Chitwan National Park, a seed bank, a sacred grove, a zoo, a buffer zone.  ·  Give one reason in-situ is preferred and one case where ex-situ is necessary.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Explain why a small isolated park can still lose a large mammal.  ·  Nepal's in-situ system dates from Chitwan National Park (1973), the country's first national park, and Sagarmatha National Park (1976), later listed as a World Heritage Site. Conservation areas such as Annapurna add community management beside strict protection.  ·  A protected area fails if it is an island. Animals that need a large range suffer inbreeding and edge effects when the reserve is small and cut off. Corridors, buffer zones and control of poaching are part of the strategy, not extras.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Sacred groves and community forests protect patches of habitat because local rules limit cutting and hunting. They are in-situ even when they are not named as national parks.  ·  # Conservation strategies — in-situ and ex-situ ## 1.
